extracted.intended_audience: judges, criminalists, detectives, and forensic investigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for assessing the character, motives, reliability, and likely behavior of suspects and witnesses through interview, observation, and analysis of life-history, habits, speech, social relations, and somatic signs. Emphasizes whole-person evaluation rather than isolated traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct, searching inquiry into the criminal's inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak with the criminal, not alone concerning the deed immediately in question, but also searchingly concerning the important conditions of his inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only by speaking with the criminal about his wishes, beliefs, and life-conditions can one proceed with approximate certainty; ask about aims, needs, pleasures, and past activities to see 'what he is' in relation to deeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview important witnesses about their ways of judging and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The same thing must also be done with regard to an important witness, especially when much depends upon his way of judging, of experiencing, of feeling, and of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a witness's outlook materially affects the case and cannot be discovered otherwise, interrogate them about their inner life; such analyses may be tiring and sometimes fruitless but can reveal wide-ranging physical and mental conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational recounting of deeds to reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: We discover what we are through what we do; discover from some person important to us what he does by simple conversation about what he has done until now and what he did lately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask subjects to recount ordinary actions and past deeds repeatedly; repeated readings/conversations let characteristic qualities emerge and corroborate conclusions when combined with other observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret judgments about others as self-revelatory
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person judges, praises or condemns others he is really talking about himself; the things he praises he does, what he faults he avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how people describe others—these utterances often aim to justify or enhance themselves and thus serve as indirect evidence of their motives and likely behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify needs and pleasures as motive indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: If we know that a real need was behind the crime, we need no longer wonder at the magnitude of the power; a man's pleasures belong also to these needs and clarify will, power, striving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate an individual's dominant needs and pleasures (broadly defined) because they often explain why a person acted and the energy behind acts; study both trivial and significant pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe behavior in presence of opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's behavior with regard to the discovered or sought-out opportunity exhibits his character wholly and completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, observe or recreate opportunities (temptations); how people act when chance appears often exposes their true character and tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate accurate self-knowledge to inform suspicion of others
rubrics_metrics.description: To observe and judge men in general the most important one is to know yourself as well as possible, for accurate self-knowledge leads to deep mistrust with regard to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-knowledge produces appropriate skepticism; this guarded stance reduces error in evaluating others but still allows acceptance when genuine good is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess manner and degree of promise-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is characterized by the way he behaves in regard to his promises; not merely keeping or breaking but the manner and degree in which a promise is kept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare promises, hopes, performance, and fears (La Roche-Foucauld): the qualitative aspects of promise behavior can illuminate reliability and complicity potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study a person's 'style' (the 'handwriting of his soul')
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought to concern oneself with a man's style—the handwriting of his soul—since education, upbringing, intelligence, softness/hardness, kindness/cruelty, determination/weakness appear in style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read manuscripts repeatedly and in different contexts; note where expressive qualities appear and cluster—these form corroborative impressions when combined with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small habitual qualities as diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain small apparently indifferent qualities and habits (never late, always carries a pencil, always wears clean clothes) are important indicators of inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and integrate numerous small observations (often from simple or longstanding acquaintances); these can combine to reveal a subject's tendencies and life-structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve observations and abstract general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge requires attention and appropriate conservation of his own observations; when series of such observations are brought together it is not difficult to generalize and to abstract specific rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep records; derive heuristics from repeated cases to be reapplied when needed—these rules have corroborative value though not standalone evidential power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze use of the pronoun 'we' to detect group affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the word 'we' indicates the opposition of a larger or smaller group of which the 'I' is a member; 'we' defines relationships from narrow to broad and can signal alliances, including criminal alliances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for involuntary 'we' formulations (e.g., 'we house-breakers'); these utterances may confess alliance or habitual association and should inform investigative lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge the whole person rather than single traits
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to suppose that it is enough in most cases to study that side of a man which is at the moment important—this leads to one-sided judgment; every individual quality is merely a symptom of a whole nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate multiple traits, life-history, and contexts; recognize interactions between 'good' and 'bad' properties (e.g., kindness arising from weakness) to avoid misleading, narrow conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer information from indifferent or low-status witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: People show their weaknesses most readily before those whom they hold of no account; servants and others of the same class often supply more important and more reliable information than authorities or friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question servants, porters, and subordinate observers deliberately—because their indifference often yields truth; do not rely solely on official or high-status testimonials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware esprit de corps and trade jealousy among expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Esprit de corps and jealousy pull the truth with frightful force; craftsmen will exaggerate or understate about fellows according to self-interest and jealousy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bias patterns: craftsmen may inflate general trade value but downplay a rival's particular strengths; treat same-trade testimony with caution and try to correct for competitive motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of self-aggrandizing narratives about past or abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people desire to appear more interesting than they are (exaggerated wild youth, achievements); those who claim 'everything is possible' or boastful feats often mislead and require caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extravagant self-portrayals skeptically; verify claims of past behavior or feats since people may invent or exaggerate to appear impressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect promoters/inventors by their propensity to deem 'everything possible'
rubrics_metrics.description: People inclined to grand projects (perpetual-motion machines, dirigible airships, panaceas) often consider everything possible and are unreliable for factual judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If suspected, draw them into discussion of a project or invention—their 'suspicious warmth' betrays class membership and unreliable cognition; distinguish this from talented persons who may exaggerate performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for demeanor changes over time (e.g., under arrest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspects under arrest often alter completely over time—become sullen, coarse, passionate, defiant, or silent; such changes may mask innocence or indicate mistreatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overinterpret changed behavior as proof of guilt; consider situational factors and whether a different approach or reevaluation is required when demeanor has shifted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate life-history and past possession/loss as motive source
rubrics_metrics.description: Many crimes spring from a past possession and subsequent loss; the motive of a deed is often rooted in the criminal's past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the subject's past—long intervals between loss and crime can culminate in actions later; search for historical attachments that explain current offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize ostensible (apparent) versus concealed motives
rubrics_metrics.description: In most capital crimes two or more motives work together, an ostensible and a concealed one; criminals use apparent motives to excuse acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek hidden motives beyond the story offered (need, self-defense claims, sexual rationalizations); be aware that subjects may self-deceive and come to believe their own excuses, complicating detection of falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between deliberate lying and self-deception
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has convinced himself of his false account watches objections with greater care and has a 'fine ear' for objections; the self-convinced are psychologically different from obvious liars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe how a subject reacts to doubts and contradictions: the self-deceived may attend more carefully to objections and are harder to disprove psychologically; adjust interrogation and evidentiary strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discussion of similar cases to test sincerity of offered motives
rubrics_metrics.description: When an accused person speaks about similar crimes where the ostensible motive was present, his defense of those acts reveals whether he truly believes his offered motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about analogous cases: defense or pardon of similar actors indicates genuine belief in the motive; inconsistency suggests ostensible justification rather than true motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider somatic character-units but avoid deterministic conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are phenomena where bodily features reflect or shape mental states (e.g., devotees appear feminine; impotents exhibit disagreeable characteristics); 'Beware of the marked one' but 'Non cum hoc, sed propter hoc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical malformations and bodily signs as possible indicators of adapted personality responses (bitterness, envy, defensive wit), while not asserting that deformity causes evil; treat somatic signs as part of a broader evidential picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social reaction to deformity in forming criminal tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Marked persons often suffer scorn and maltreatment from childhood leading to bitterness, envy, joy in destruction and other tendencies that may aggregate into criminal dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate social history of stigma—repeated abuse or exclusion often shapes adaptive behaviors (wit, suspicion, cruelty) which can be relevant to motive and character analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize compensatory intellectual development among the stigmatized
rubrics_metrics.description: Marked persons are often wiser or better-instructed because deformity compels them into solitary, reflective pursuits and training of wits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance assumptions: somatic stigma may correlate with higher intellectual adaptation and cunning; incorporate such compensatory traits into assessments rather than presuming solely degeneracy.
